title: Ministers
hookLine: bishops, priests, deacons, pastors, elders; churches differ on ordaining women, some do and some don't

cards: The problem was the food line. In the sixth chapter of Acts, the church in Jerusalem shares meals with widows every day, and the Greek-speaking believers complain that their widows are being overlooked.
The apostles can't preach and run the kitchen too. So the church chooses seven men, of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, to see that the food is shared fairly.
Then a small, physical moment churches still repeat: "when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them." Hands on heads, to send people out to serve tables.

teach.h: SET APART BY PRAYER AND HANDS.
teach.b: Ordination is the church setting someone apart for a ministry, usually with prayer and the laying on of hands.
Paul reminds Timothy of it: "Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery." A gift given through other people's hands.

teach.h: THE FIRST HANDS SENT PEOPLE TO SERVE.
teach.b: And the first hands in Acts weren't for a throne. They were for a kitchen. The titles vary.

Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches ordain bishops, priests and deacons. Catholics and the Orthodox count holy orders as a sacrament, and Catholic teaching says it leaves a lasting mark on the person ordained.
Lutheran, Reformed, Methodist and Baptist churches ordain pastors, ministers, elders and deacons, and often describe ordination as the church recognizing and confirming a call God has already given.
And here churches differ in a way that matters deeply to people on every side: whether women may be ordained.
The Catholic and Orthodox churches ordain only men as priests and bishops, holding that they follow Christ's own choice of apostles.
Some Protestant and Anglican churches ordain women as pastors, priests and bishops, pointing to women like Phebe, whom Paul calls "a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea."
Other Protestant churches, including some Baptist and Reformed ones, ordain only men as pastors, reading Paul's letters to Timothy as setting that pattern.
Traditions differ, and each side reads scripture seriously and holds its answer with care. What these ordinations share is in that first scene: hands, prayer, and a job to do for others.

how: In churches across traditions a person is ordained in a service of prayer with the laying on of hands, by a bishop in Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches, or by ministers and elders in other Protestant churches; churches differ on whether women may be ordained.

games.q: you're an apostle in Jerusalem. widows are being overlooked in the daily food. what do you do?
o: stop preaching and run the kitchen yourself.
have the church choose people to serve, pray, and lay hands on them.
tell the widows to sort it out themselves.
games.why: the church chose seven, and "when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them." the first hands sent people to serve.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has served in a church, a priest at a hospital bed, a pastor who remembered your name, a deacon at the door, a chaplain; if no one comes, think of anyone whose job is to look after other people's hearts.
Remember one specific thing they did, and let the gratitude be specific too. If you pray, give thanks for them by name; if you don't, simply hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Ordination. Setting someone apart for ministry, with prayer and the laying on of hands, to serve.

orig.note: Greek: to appoint — used in Acts 14:23, where the King James says Paul and Barnabas "ordained them elders."
